explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Jesus says the opposite. He says, “This sickness will not end in death.” That's the very first thing out of His mouth when He hears the news. It's an easy one to flip in your head, and I've flipped worse, like the time I mixed up the salt and the sugar jars in my own bakery.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” He says it plainly as soon as He hears. Keep that sentence in your back pocket, because this story has a few twists coming.

explanations.answer: The glory of God and His Son
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus says, “…it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” He names God and the Son of God right there. It's the reason He gives, and I'll stick to what He actually said.

explanations.answer: A test of the sisters' trust
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says the sickness is “…for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” The text doesn't call it a test of Mary and Martha. Honestly, a test is the first thing I'd have reached for too, so you're in good company.

explanations.answer: A lesson for the whole village
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, but a village lesson isn't what Jesus says. He doesn't mention the village at all. What He says is that it's “…for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” That's the whole reason He gives, and I bet a few of us would've added a few more reasons of our own.

explanations.answer: Stays where He is for two days
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. John says that on hearing Lazarus was sick, Jesus “…stayed where He was for two days…” It's a surprising thing to read right after the story says He loved this family. John doesn't hand us a reason for the wait, so I won't invent one. I'll just say I think it makes you lean in and keep reading.

explanations.answer: Leaves for Bethany that same hour
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, friend, because that's what I'd expect from someone who loves them. But the text says He stayed where He was for two days. Only after that does He tell the disciples, “Let us go back to Judea.” No same-hour dash to Bethany here.

That would be a tidy plan, friend, but John doesn't tell us anything like it. He says Jesus “…stayed where He was for two days…” After that, He speaks to the disciples about going back to Judea. No scouting party in this story.

You got it, friend. The disciples say, “the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?” That's the text's own word for it, and it tells you how recent the danger was. They aren't being rude, I think they're worried. When they speak up, it comes out as a question.

The text says the opposite, friend. When Jesus says to go back to Judea, the disciples answer, “Rabbi, the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?” So they do remind Him, and right away. I think that one question holds all their worry.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “If anyone walks in the daytime, he will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world.” Then He turns it around: whoever walks at night will stumble, because he has no light. Walking by daylight means you can see where your feet are going.

I like the thought, friend, but worry isn't the word Jesus uses. He says the one who walks in the daytime “…will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world.” The trouble He talks about is tripping, not fretting. Your feet are the ones in danger here.

Not quite, friend. Hiding never comes up in this saying. Jesus says whoever walks in the daytime “…will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world.” It's all about being able to see where you're walking.

explanations.answer: Go there and wake him up
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus says, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up.” Notice He calls Lazarus “our friend,” and He's the one doing the going. The disciples have a hard time following what He means by it, as the next verses show.

explanations.answer: Let him rest a while longer
explanations.explanation: That makes sense if you take the sleep as plain sleep, friend, and the disciples did exactly that. But Jesus says, “…I am going there to wake him up.” He doesn't plan to leave Lazarus resting. He plans to go.

explanations.answer: Pray for him from right here
explanations.explanation: A kind idea, friend, but that isn't what Jesus says. He tells the disciples, “…I am going there to wake him up.” He's talking about traveling to Lazarus, not staying put. Praying from here never comes up in this passage.

That's right, friend. The disciples reply, “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better.” It's perfectly sensible if sleep means sleep. They just don't know yet what Jesus really means, and John explains it in the next verse.

The text says they did, friend. His disciples reply, “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better.” They heard “sleep” and took it as plain sleep. John tells us right after that Jesus meant something else.

Yes, friend. John says the disciples “…thought that Jesus was talking about actual sleep, but He was speaking about the death of Lazarus.” John steps in to clear it up for us. Jesus will say it in plain words in the very next verse.

Creative, friend, but no dream appears in this story. John says Jesus “…was speaking about the death of Lazarus.” The disciples took Him to mean actual sleep, and the real meaning was far heavier. I think this part of the story hurts.

I see how you got there, friend, but the text says something else. John says Jesus “…was speaking about the death of Lazarus.” Then Jesus makes it plain Himself: “Lazarus is dead…” Hope never comes up in this passage.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “…for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe.” He's speaking straight to the disciples, and He says “…for your sake…” That's the reason He gives, so that's the one I'll hold onto.

explanations.answer: So the sisters may learn patience
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd guess that, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He tells the disciples, “…for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe.” The reason He gives is about the disciples believing. Patience isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So the crowds may stay away
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, friend, but crowds don't come up in these verses. Jesus says, “…for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe.” The “you” is the disciples he's talking to. Their believing is the whole reason He names.
Not so, friend. Right after telling them Lazarus is dead, Jesus says, “But let us go to him.” He doesn't say there's no reason to go. If anything, He's the one getting everybody moving.
That's right, friend. Jesus finishes His words with, “But let us go to him.” Lazarus is dead, and He still says to go. That little “But” is carrying a lot of weight.

explanations.answer: Let us also go so that we may die with Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Thomas, the disciple also called Didymus, says to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.” He knows the danger in Judea, since they'd just reminded Jesus about the stoning. I think those are the words of a man who isn't backing out. He's ready to go with Jesus, and that's a lot of courage.

explanations.answer: Let us stay here until it is safe to travel
explanations.explanation: That would be the careful choice, friend, but it isn't what Thomas says. Thomas, a disciple also called Didymus, tells his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.” He talks about going, not waiting. The text doesn't show anyone suggesting a delay.

explanations.answer: Let us send word to the sisters before we go
explanations.explanation: A thoughtful idea, friend, but no one says it here. Thomas, also called Didymus, says to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.” Nothing about sending word ahead. He just says they should all go.
